frameworks.name: Three-Step GMB Ranking Formula
frameworks.definition: A three-stage process for ranking first on Google Maps without a website: (1) market research to select cities by search volume and competition, (2) on-page GMB SEO optimization combined with review-count parity, (3) ongoing maintenance to preserve rank.
frameworks.concept: Geographic Expansion Sequence: Dominate Local, Then Expand

claims.text: The host (Plumber Done Right) argues that a Google My Business (GMB) website is not the primary ranking factor for Google Maps placement; a GMB profile with as few as two three-star reviews will receive no calls regardless of how strong the associated website is. On-page GMB profile optimization and review count dominate ranking weight relative to website SEO.
claims.speaker: the host (Plumber Done Right)
claims.speaker_term: on page SEO specifically the SEO that's done on your google business profile
conditions: Local service businesses (e.g., plumbing) in competitive urban markets
Google Maps / Google My Business ranking context
claims.mechanism: Google Maps ranking algorithm weights GMB profile completeness and review signals more heavily than website domain authority for local search; website authority improves rank but is not the binding constraint.
bounded_by: Website SEO and GMB profile do work together; website is not irrelevant, only not the primary constraint

claims.text: For Google Maps local service ranking (e.g., plumbing in Canadian cities), a threshold of at least 400 monthly searches for the target keyword in a given city is the minimum viable market worth prioritizing. Cities below 400 monthly searches are worth entering only if competition is negligible.

claims.text: To rank in the Google Maps top three for a local service keyword, a GMB profile must have a review count within approximately 20% of the third-place ranked profile's review count; below that threshold, on-page SEO improvements cannot fully compensate for the review-count gap.

claims.mechanism: Google's ranking algorithm uses review count as a trust and authority signal; being too far below competitors' review counts cannot be overcome by keyword optimization alone, because review volume acts as a social-proof filter baked into the algorithm.

examples.text: The host (Plumber Done Right) demonstrated his GMB ranking methodology live using Oshawa, Ontario as a case study. Searching 'plumber Oshawa' in SEMrush showed approximately 2,800 related monthly searches, reduced to roughly 2,000 high-intent searches after subtracting branded/company-specific queries. The top competitor had 1,300 reviews and a 4.9-star rating, which the host deemed very difficult to beat outright. The second competitor had 180 reviews and 4.8 stars. The host identified that this competitor used 'plumbing' rather than 'plumber' as their primary keyword and had inconsistent recent reviews (a week ago and two months ago), meaning the effective review bar to outrank them dropped from 180 to approximately 100 after factoring in SEO advantages. The host's own Oshawa profile had 105 reviews, ranked second overall, and generated approximately 10-15 leads per week.

The host (Plumber Done Right) showed a Brampton, Ontario GMB profile ranking first for plumbing searches in a city with over 800,000 residents. He verified ownership by showing the profile phone number matched a number he controls, generating approximately 20 leads per week from that profile alone. A second unnamed profile also ranked first but was not emphasized. A Richmond Hill profile was shown managed under his GMB account with full manager access, further demonstrating the multi-profile replication model across the Greater Toronto Area.

The host (Plumber Done Right) acknowledged his Oshawa GMB profile had only about 58% of the review count of the third-place competitor (105 vs. 180 reviews), which fell below his stated 20% parity rule (which would require 144 reviews). He attributes his second-place ranking despite this shortfall to a superior star rating and stronger on-page keyword optimization, demonstrating that the 20% rule is a floor that SEO can partially compensate for in practice.

practices.text: Use SEMrush (or equivalent keyword tool) to look up monthly search volumes for '[service] + [city name]' in your target geography before investing in a GMB profile for that city.

Fill out every section of the GMB profile completely: description with high-intent keywords (e.g., 'plumber near me in [city]', 'emergency plumber', '24 hours'), product listings, service descriptions with keyword-rich copy, Q&A section, service areas with specific postal codes, and regular photo posts.

Analyze the consistency of competitors' recent reviews (recency signal) when estimating the effective review count needed to outrank them; infrequent recent reviews reduce the effective bar even if total review count is high.

Post updates to your GMB profile once every one to two weeks and add new products periodically to maintain freshness signals; treat this as a 10-minute-per-week task once top-three ranking is achieved.

practices.text: Source reviews through creative low-cost means: asking friends and family with payment incentives (~$2-5 per review), hiring someone to approach people at college campuses or malls to request reviews via a shared link, rather than buying bulk reviews from overseas vendors (which are deleted by Google).

Prioritize cities with high search volume and low competitor review counts first; once those are ranked, expand to lower-volume cities as a secondary tranche since even small cities add marginal leads that accumulate across a portfolio of profiles.
